title: Tuladhara's honest scale
hookLine: a great ascetic is sent to a market stall to learn dharma
carry: dharma lives at an honest counter too

cards: A man stands in the forest so still, for so long, that a pair of birds builds a nest in his matted hair. That's how the Mahabharata tells it. His name is Jajali, an ascetic.
The birds lay their eggs. The eggs hatch. He stays still until the chicks grow wings, fly off, and stop coming back.
Then a thought arrives, and it's a proud one: who in the world is my equal in dharma? An unseen voice answers. Not you, Jajali.
There's a merchant in Varanasi named Tuladhara, and you are not his equal.

teach.h: TULADHARA TELLS JAJALI HIS OWN STORY.
teach.b: So Jajali goes to Varanasi and finds him, a trader selling goods in the market. Before Jajali can say a word, Tuladhara greets him and tells him his own story: the stillness, the birds, the proud thought, the voice.
Jajali asks how a trader could know this. Tuladhara's answer, in paraphrase, is the teaching.
He knows the ancient dharma, he says, and he names it plainly: friendship toward all beings, and a way of living that harms them as little as it can. He earns his bread by trade, and keeps it honest.
He doesn't cheat on the weight. He doesn't flatter or run anyone down to make a sale. He holds the same even scale for everyone who comes to his counter.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE SCALES.
teach.b: In Sanskrit, a tula is a balance, and Tuladhara can be heard as the one who holds the scales. In this story, the scale on the counter and the evenness in his mind are one practice. Now notice who's teaching whom.
The great ascetic walks all the way to a market to learn from a man who weighs things for a living. The Mahabharata doesn't tell Jajali to open a shop, or call his years in the forest a waste.
It says dharma was already sitting at that counter, in an honest weight handed to a customer Tuladhara might never see again. That's the teaching: dharma isn't only for forests and temples.
Honest work, done without harm, can itself be dharma and seva.

how: Hindu teachers sometimes retell the dialogue of Tuladhara and Jajali from the Mahabharata to show that honest work in an ordinary trade can itself be a way of dharma.

o: a merchant's vow to give up selling
charity given on top of a day's trade
service done through the honest work itself

games.q: the merchant and the ascetic — tap the pairs.
p: the ascetic with birds in his hair
a balance, a pair of scales

s: Tuladhara tells Jajali to leave the forest and open a shop
the story doesn't say that. it shows dharma already at work behind an honest counter.
Tuladhara knows Jajali's story before Jajali tells it
he greets him and recounts the stillness, the birds and the proud thought.
in the story, the ascetic teaches the merchant
it's the other way around: Jajali walks to Varanasi to learn from Tuladhara.

games.q: you're Jajali. birds have just raised their chicks in your hair, and a voice says a merchant knows dharma better than you. what do you do?
o: dismiss it: a shopkeeper can't know dharma.
go to Varanasi and find him.
stand still even longer to prove the voice wrong.
games.why: he goes to the market, and the merchant greets him with his own story. the teacher he needs is behind a counter.

practice: Rest your hands palm up on your knees, like the two pans of a balance, and bring to mind one exchange waiting for you: a sale, a report, a favor, a reply.
Notice where you'd be tempted to tip it a little, a corner cut, a bit of flattery, then let both hands rest evenly again and breathe there. If you pray, you can offer that exchange to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: Seva as vocation. Service done through the work itself, the way Tuladhara served everyone who trusted his scales.

orig.note: Sanskrit tulādhāra, the one who holds the scales: the merchant of Varanasi who teaches Jajali dharma in the Mahabharata.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma lives at an honest counter too. A scale held level serves every buyer who trusts it, whether or not anyone notices. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva (Moksha-dharma section), the dialogue of Tuladhara and Jajali
